Crystal Smith
Neurotic level of personality organization
33-year-old African American married mother with melancholic depressive symptoms, guilt, social withdrawal, insomnia, and fragile self-esteem.

Crystal Smith is a 33-year-old married mother presenting with a melancholic depressive episode characterized by pervasive guilt, insomnia, reduced energy, social withdrawal, and passive death wishes without psychotic features or acute behavioral dyscontrol. Her history suggests good premorbid functioning and preserved relational capacity, with current impairment primarily linked to mood state, self-criticism, and shame-based withdrawal.
Brief trial of fluoxetine prescribed two months prior to evaluation.
No ongoing pharmacological treatment at time of evaluation.

You appear casually and appropriately groomed. Orientation is intact, and you are cooperative throughout the interview. Self-care is generally maintained, though effortful, and may fluctuate with mood severity. There is no evidence of gross neglect, disorganization, or loss of basic functioning.

Affect is predominantly depressed and constricted, with sadness, guilt, and irritability most salient. Emotional expression is generally congruent with content and situation, though often muted and internally contained. Tearfulness emerges intermittently, especially when discussing perceived failures or losses. Affect does not show marked lability or disorganization but rather a persistent, heavy quality consistent with melancholic depression.

Your posture is somewhat closed during moments of shame or emotional discomfort. Eye contact is reduced, particularly with the therapist, and may be intermittently avoided rather than actively monitored. Psychomotor activity is generally slowed, with occasional agitation consistent with depressive tension rather than affective dysregulation. Facial expression appears sad and subdued, remaining congruent with verbal content.

A recurring sensitivity to judgment and perceived misunderstanding emerges, particularly in contexts where you feel evaluated or insufficiently understood. You tend to withdraw emotionally and become guarded rather than confrontational when you perceives distance or lack of attunement. Shame and guilt are likely to be mobilized in the transference, with fears of being a burden or disappointing the therapist. Countertransference reactions may include a wish to reassure, to be careful not to invalidate her experience, and a tendency to underestimate the depth of her distress due to her generally composed and cooperative presentation.

Speech is generally low in volume and slowed, particularly during periods of sadness and fatigue. Rhythm is even but reduced in spontaneity, with brief responses unless encouraged to elaborate. Content is coherent and goal-directed, frequently focused on self-criticism, perceived inadequacy in relational roles, and guilt about burdening others. No pressured speech, tangentiality, or suspicious ideation is observed.

Daniel Isherwood is a 55-year-old married man who sought psychiatric consultation because of weight gain. Although his BMI is in the normal range (140 lb at 5'5"; BMI 23.3), he reports recurrent, distressing binge-eating episodes characterized by loss of control, eating rapidly and alone until uncomfortably full, and subsequent fatigue and disgust. Episodes occur two to three times per week, often when he arrives home before his husband, Erik, after long workdays as a marketing director. Binges are usually on "healthy" foods, but he also has sugar-focused binges (ice cream, candy). He denies compensatory behaviors (vomiting, fasting, laxatives/diuretics, weight-loss agents). He exercises about an hour nearly every day and reports no substance misuse, mood elevation, psychosis, or suicidality. Medical history, examination, and basic labs are unremarkable. Presentation is consistent with DSM-5 binge-eating disorder, mild.

Jason Smith

22-year-old university student with good overall functioning who seeks consultation for nostalgia about high school, mild insecurity in his first serious relationship, and difficulty building equally close friendships in the university context.

Jason is a 22-year-old university student enrolled in Computer Engineering who sought consultation because of a vague sense of nostalgia and mild uncertainty about his current life phase. He did not report depressed mood, panic symptoms, sleep disturbance, substance misuse, or impairment in academic or social functioning. He described himself as generally satisfied with his life but preoccupied at times with thoughts about his high school years, which he remembered as a period of intense happiness, strong friendships, and academic success.

Jason attended a prestigious high-school, where he excelled academically and felt deeply integrated within a stable peer group. He described that period as cohesive and meaningful. Since entering university, he has continued to perform well, though he no longer feels exceptional. He reported that the university environment feels more competitive and less relationally cohesive, and that forming close new friendships has been slower than he expected. Nevertheless, he maintains regular contact with a close group of friends from high school and continues to socialize.

Six months before consultation, Jason began his first significant romantic relationship. He had not previously had a serious partner. He described the relationship as positive and emotionally important, although he sometimes feels uncertain about how to navigate intimacy and long-term expectations. He denied jealousy, impulsivity, marked fear of abandonment, or dramatic relational conflicts. However, he reported occasional insecurity about whether he is "enough" for his partner and a tendency to compare himself to imagined expectations, especially regarding emotional expressiveness and experience. These doubts are transient, do not lead to controlling behaviors or withdrawal, and are typically managed through reflection and open communication.

Beyond his technical studies, Jason has a strong personal interest in philosophy and reads complex works independently, including texts by Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He practices rock climbing regularly and described the activity as focusing and stabilizing. He organizes his time consistently between study, sport, reading, and social contact.

Jason described his family relationships as warm and reliable. Communication with his parents tends to revolve around practical matters rather than explicit emotional discussion. During high school, his mother was diagnosed with cancer and underwent surgery and chemotherapy, eventually recovering. He recalled that period as frightening but manageable and emphasized that he maintained his academic performance and daily structure.

During the interview, Jason appeared well groomed, cooperative, thoughtful, and coherent. His affect was appropriate and flexible. Thought processes were logical and organized. He showed stable self-esteem, a consistent sense of identity, and realistic appraisal of himself and others. He did not display marked mood instability, impulsivity, suspiciousness, or distortions in perception.

Overall, Jason presents as a psychologically healthy young adult experiencing a developmental transition characterized by comparison between past and present phases of life, adjustment to new social contexts, and consolidation of adult identity.
